findings.text: Native signal and restart handling on return to user. When entry follows a system call it records distinct continue and restart addresses, clears recorded call state so the return path does not restart again, and pre-adjusts saved return value and program position for restartable outcomes. It then checks for a deliverable signal and either dispatches it, possibly cancelling the restart first, or completes restart-block handling and restores the saved mask.

Restart is honoured only when the saved program position still equals the computed restart address, showing no debugger redirection. Cancellation to interruption applies for no-handler and restart-block outcomes and for restartable calls whose disposition lacks restart permission; otherwise the pre-adjustment stands. The non-signal path installs restart-block handling for the restart-block outcome and rewinds single-step state.
Native signal interface exposes a return-to-user handler for restart and delivery plus a read-only-after-init minimum signal stack size value consumed by signal stack management.

Compat floating point signal frame is eight byte aligned and ordered as magic word, size word, thirty two double slots plus a status control word grouped as user area, then exception flag and two instruction words grouped as exception area. The auxiliary frame contains this VFP area followed by a terminal word chosen to avoid collision with any coprocessor magic.

Compat VFP ABI markers are magic hexadecimal 56465001, storage size equal to the full VFP frame size, and fault status write shift eleven. Restore validates incoming magic and size against expected values and rejects mismatch as invalid argument.

128 bit register view pairs a raw wide value with an ordered pair of halves whose high and low positions swap between big-endian and little-endian builds, allowing two adjacent compat double slots to be assembled into one native vector register in order.

Compat VFP restore requires exact magic and size, merges each adjacent pair of double slots into successive native vector registers, derives native status and control words by masking the compat control word with status and control masks, and only after successful user reads flushes current hardware state before installing the assembled state into the thread.

Compat frame restore merges two 32 bit mask words into one native blocked set and installs it when the user copy succeeds, restores general registers including frame and intra-procedure slots plus stack link program and status with status converted from compat to native form, clears restart state, validates user register state, and restores VFP from auxiliary space only when validation passes and hardware supports it.

Compat return-from-signal entries force pending restarted calls to report interruption, require eight byte stack alignment and a fully accessible frame, restore the saved context and for the real-time variant also the alternate stack, return the restored first argument register on success, and otherwise notify a fault at the stack pointer and return zero.

Compat restore hazards include misaligned stack or inaccessible frame leading to fault notification, mismatched VFP magic or size leading to invalid argument, failed user copies leading to fault status, invalid user register state failing validation, and stale restart state if the forced no-restart action were omitted.

Low level resume entries re-establish execution after sleep. The first initializes exception level and processor setup, enables translation with swapper and identity tables to reach saved state by virtual address, then transfers to the second. The second finalizes higher exception level, selects per-processor context by hashed hardware identifier, restores stack and system state, optionally clears stack poisoning, restores callee saved registers, and returns success.

Resume progresses from mode init through processor setup and early translation enable, to context lookup by identifier hash and stash table, to system restore through the context pointer, to sanitizer handling where configured, to callee register restore and return. Translation must be active before stash access by virtual address, and stack must be restored before system resume.

Firmware call trampolines expose distinct symbols for SMC, HVC, and version 1.2 HVC conduits, each delegating to a shared conduit macro that preserves the calling convention for arguments and results.

Secondary coordination state comprises a global handoff record for idle task and boot status, a stuck-processor counter, read-only-after-init interrupt base and count, a descriptor table sized by maximum interrupts held per processor, and flags selecting per-processor descriptors and recording crash stop.

Processor bring-up publishes idle task and translation-off status, invokes firmware-specific boot, waits bounded time for online completion, and on timeout clears the handoff, samples late versus early status, classifies unknown, killed, stuck, or panic states with distinct diagnostics including address size and granule reasons, accounts stuck processors, and reports failure; timely online reports success.

Firmware operation wrappers delegate boot, kill, and disable to per-processor operation tables, reporting not-supported when the hook is absent. One kill configuration unconditionally reports not-supported while the other assumes death when no kill hook exists and otherwise delegates.

Secondary initialization takes a reference on the initial address space and activates it, removes the identity mapping, optionally initializes interrupt priority masking, announces to runtime tracking with interrupts off, enforces capability match, runs firmware post-boot hook, records processor info and topology, enables interrupt and timer subsystems, sets up per-processor interrupts and NUMA association, then publishes online state and completion before restoring processor flags and entering idle.

Processor offline requires firmware die support and optional disable approval, then withdraws topology and NUMA association, irreversibly clears online state, tears down per-processor interrupts, and migrates interrupts away. Dead-processor cleanup afterwards attempts firmware kill and warns if the processor may still be active.

Interrupt teardown iterates over the configured interrupt count and either disables shared per-processor interrupts or non-maskable variants, or disables the per-processor descriptor interrupt without waiting when descriptors are per processor, and warns once if no interrupt base was established.

Priority masking setup enables system register access for the distributor, asserts that interrupt and fast interrupt masks are set in current flags, then programs the priority mask to the enabled value with interrupt-pending behavior.

Boot completion and preparation entries log activation counts, report whether processors started at elevated or normal level or mismatched with taint, apply hypervisor layout and relocations when virtualization is enabled but kernel is outside hypervisor mode, establish system and user capabilities, protect the linear alias of text, and for the boot processor switch to runtime per-processor storage and initialize sanitizer tag state.

Symmetric multiprocessing interface exposes bring-up, takedown, secondary entry, dead-processor cleanup, boot completion, boot-processor preparation, and ACPI registration and mapping operations plus the secondary handoff record for cross-file coordination.

Linear alias protection removes write permission from the alias covering executable and read-only regions up to init begin, and when hibernation with read-only data is enabled registers a power notifier to restore writable alias for snapshot. Mapping updates reject virtual addresses below the kernel base with a warning, otherwise create the page entry and invalidate kernel translation entries over the range.

ACPI processor registration defers when the processor handle is missing under hotplug builds, rejects changes to present bits as unsupported, records hot-pluggability from architecture policy, and registers the processor device. Unregistration warns once on present-bit removal indicated by status evaluation before unregistering.

MADT mapping skips disabled entries lacking enable or online-capable flags, rejects identifiers outside the hardware mask or equal to invalid sentinel and duplicates including boot-processor duplicates, records the boot processor once, otherwise assigns the next logical identifier, copies the controller entry, initializes mailbox parking data, and advances the count. Parsing validates entry bounds before mapping, and presence query either tests the enabled flag or reports absent by build.

Bring-up and mapping hazards include timeout without online status leaving a processor counted as stuck, unsupported configuration causing panic, firmware kill failure leaving questionable shutdown, mapping updates outside kernel range being refused, and duplicate or invalid MADT identifiers being skipped with loss of a processor.
